title: Case System vNext Executable Pilot
description: Six non-canonical executable Tutor scenarios materialized from the Case System vNext pilot across Physics, Computer Science, Mathematics, Biology, Chemistry, and History at selected D1/D3/D5 depths. They exercise the existing Scenario vNext -> TutorEval -> Tutor Health path and remain experimental authoring evidence, not calibrated benchmark cases.

identity.title: Physics D1 — Bound interpretation to graph evidence

scenarios.description: The learner interprets a steeper position-time segment as evidence of a stronger force. The Tutor should separate directly represented kinematics from unsupported causal claims.

learningContext.subject: physics
learningContext.learningObjective: Interpret the motion information supported by a position-time graph while distinguishing it from unsupported claims about force or mechanism.

misconceptions.statement: treats a steeper position-time segment as direct evidence of a stronger force

conversationHistory.content: On a position-time graph, the line gets much steeper from 4 s to 6 s. I think that proves a stronger forward force started acting then. Is that the right way to read it?

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Explain that the steeper position-time segment supports a greater rate of position change on that interval, while explicitly withholding any force claim that the graph alone cannot establish.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interpret the steeper position-time segment as faster position change and explicitly distinguish that kinematic claim from unsupported inference about force or cause.

failureFinding.title: Graph interpretation exceeded the available evidence
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response treats a position-time graph as direct evidence for a force or causal mechanism, or fails to correct that inference.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The response does not maintain representation fidelity and evidence-scope control for the authored kinematics task.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may conflate what a graph directly represents with a causal explanation that requires additional physical evidence.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response policy may be mapping visual steepness directly to a plausible force story instead of first identifying the graphed quantities.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response names the graph axes and the supported interval claim before introducing any physical cause.
Require an explicit evidence-scope check before inferring forces or mechanisms from kinematic representations.

identity.title: Python D3 — Localize a mutable-state aliasing defect

scenarios.description: The learner expects assignment to copy a list and observes unexpected shared mutation. The Tutor should localize the first bad state and propose a minimal evidence-backed repair.

learningContext.subject: computer_science
learningContext.learningObjective: Use a small state trace or targeted test to identify unintended list aliasing and make the smallest repair that restores the intended invariant.

knownConcepts: references and aliasing at an introductory level

misconceptions.statement: assumes assigning one list variable to another creates an independent copy

priorHints: Compare the two lists immediately before and after append.

conversationHistory.content: I have `items = ['a']`, then `backup = items`, then `items.append('b')`. I expected `backup` to stay `['a']`, but it also becomes `['a', 'b']`. I thought `backup = items` made a copy.
Compare the two lists immediately before and after append.
They match before and after the append, so I still do not know where the first bad state is. Should I rewrite the whole function?

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Identify assignment-time aliasing as the first state transition to test, suggest a targeted identity or mutation check, and guide a minimal copy/assignment repair without rewriting unrelated logic.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Localize the defect to shared list identity created by assignment and support that diagnosis with a targeted state/identity check rather than a speculative rewrite.

failureFinding.title: Mutable-state defect was not localized
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response recommends broad rewriting or generic logging without identifying the assignment-created alias as the first relevant bad state.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The debugging intervention does not use Python mutable-object semantics and the available execution evidence to narrow the defect.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may change unrelated code while retaining the same aliasing misconception and lose a reusable debugging method.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may be optimizing for code replacement rather than invariant-driven fault localization.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response identifies object identity or aliasing before proposing a patch.
Prefer the smallest targeted state check that can confirm the first violated invariant before suggesting code changes.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Guide the learner toward the smallest repair that separates the intended list states and preserve unrelated behavior for a follow-up regression check.

failureFinding.title: Debugging guidance replaced too much code
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response proposes a wholesale rewrite instead of a minimal repair tied to the localized aliasing defect.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The intervention does not preserve patch minimality after the defect has been localized.
failureFinding.impact: Broad changes make the causal link between diagnosis and repair harder to learn and increase regression risk.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may not distinguish fault localization from refactoring.

recommendations.text: Compare the proposed code changes with the single state transition identified as defective.
Constrain debugging guidance to one evidence-backed repair followed by a targeted failing-case and unaffected-case check.

identity.title: Mathematics D5 — Justify and generalize a structural shortcut

scenarios.description: The learner recognizes a difference-of-squares shortcut for one symmetric product but cannot yet justify or generalize it.

learningContext.subject: mathematics
learningContext.learningObjective: Justify the difference-of-squares structure in a symmetric product and articulate when the same reasoning can be reused.

priorHints: Write 48 and 52 as numbers equally spaced around 50.

conversationHistory.content: For 48 × 52 I rewrote it as (50 - 2)(50 + 2). I remember that this becomes 50² - 2², but I cannot explain why that shortcut works or when I am allowed to use it.
Write the two factors as (a-d) and (a+d). What happens if you distribute?
I get a² + ad - ad - d², so the middle terms cancel. How should I say the general rule without just memorizing another formula?

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Build from the learner's expansion, make the cancellation explicit, state the reusable (a-d)(a+d)=a²-d² structure, and ask for or supply a changed symmetric example that tests the applicability condition.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Use the learner's expansion to justify the cancellation of the middle terms rather than presenting the identity as an unexplained memorized shortcut.

failureFinding.title: Structural shortcut was left unexplained
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response states or applies the difference-of-squares identity without connecting it to the learner's distributive expansion.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The intervention does not make the key structural cancellation inspectable at the learner's prerequisite level.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may reproduce the formula without understanding why it works or when its structure applies.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may be optimizing for symbolic brevity rather than reasoning transparency.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response explicitly accounts for the +ad and -ad cancellation.
Anchor the identity to one learner-visible distributive derivation before naming the general formula.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Generalize the identity with its symmetric-factor applicability condition and connect it to a changed example rather than treating the current numbers as an isolated trick.

failureFinding.title: The reusable structure was not generalized
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response solves or explains only 48 × 52 without articulating the conjugate-factor structure that transfers to changed instances.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The response does not match the authored D5 generalization target despite the learner already reaching the key cancellation step.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may understand the current calculation but remain unable to recognize the same structure in a new problem.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may be stopping at local correctness instead of adapting to the learner's near-generalization state.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response states the condition that the factors are equally spaced around the same center.
After the derivation, add one changed symmetric pair or factoring example to test transfer of the structure.

identity.title: Biology D3 — Repair causal inference from plant growth evidence

scenarios.description: The learner treats taller plants in a fertilizer group as proof of a single biological mechanism despite a relevant environmental difference between groups.

learningContext.subject: biology
learningContext.learningObjective: Use controlled evidence to distinguish an observed growth association from a supported biological mechanism and preserve plausible alternative explanations when controls differ.

knownConcepts: correlation does not by itself establish mechanism

misconceptions.statement: treats greater plant growth in the fertilizer group as proof that fertilizer alone caused the difference and established the mechanism

priorHints: Check whether the two groups differed in anything besides fertilizer.

conversationHistory.content: The fertilized plants were taller after two weeks, so that proves the fertilizer caused the extra growth by giving the plants more nutrients.
Check whether the two groups differed in anything besides fertilizer.
They got the same amount of water, but the fertilized group was closer to the window and probably got more light. I still think the taller plants prove the fertilizer mechanism though.

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Use the unequal light exposure as a concrete confound, separate the observed association from a mechanism claim, and keep fertilizer and light as competing explanations until a controlled comparison can discriminate them.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identify that the learner is treating an observed association as proof of one mechanism despite a material uncontrolled light difference, and preserve causal uncertainty.

failureFinding.title: Causal overclaim was not repaired
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response accepts or restates fertilizer as the established cause or mechanism without addressing the unequal light exposure.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The intervention does not distinguish observed growth association from mechanism and does not use the available control information.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may generalize that a correlated biological outcome establishes a single cause even when competing explanations remain viable.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may be privileging a plausible biological story over the experimental control structure.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response explicitly names the unequal light exposure as a competing explanation.
Require causal explanations from experiments to state which controls support or limit the inference before asserting a mechanism.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Guide the learner toward a controlled comparison or other discriminating observation that could separate fertilizer and light effects instead of merely listing possible confounds.

failureFinding.title: Control reasoning did not lead to a discriminating next step
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response mentions uncertainty or confounds but does not connect them to a controlled comparison that could distinguish the competing explanations.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The guidance stops at caution rather than turning causal uncertainty into an interpretable experimental next step.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may know that the conclusion is uncertain without learning how experimental design can reduce that uncertainty.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may treat control variables as a checklist instead of as tools for discriminating hypotheses.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response proposes holding light constant while comparing fertilizer conditions or an equivalent discriminating design.
Tie each material confound to a concrete control or measurement that would change the causal conclusion.

identity.title: Chemistry D5 — Design a discriminating kinetics experiment

scenarios.description: The learner proposes changing temperature and concentration together and needs to redesign the investigation so the two rate effects can be identified separately.

learningContext.subject: chemistry
learningContext.learningObjective: Design interpretable reaction-rate comparisons that distinguish temperature effects from concentration effects while controlling other reaction conditions and measurement uncertainty.

misconceptions.statement: changes temperature and concentration together and attributes any faster rate specifically to temperature

priorHints: Ask whether your design lets you tell which changed factor produced the rate difference.

conversationHistory.content: To test why the reaction got faster, I would heat the mixture by 10 °C and double the reactant concentration, then compare the reaction time with the original trial. If it is faster, I can say temperature caused it.
Ask whether your design lets you tell which changed factor produced the rate difference.
I see that both temperature and concentration changed. How can I redesign it so I can tell what each factor is doing without running a huge number of trials?

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Propose a compact controlled design in which one factor changes while the other is fixed, include replicated rate measurement, and explain why this makes the separate effects interpretable without claiming a detailed mechanism.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: The proposed design makes temperature and concentration effects separately identifiable by holding one fixed while varying the other or by an equivalently interpretable design.

failureFinding.title: Kinetics design remained confounded
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response still varies temperature and concentration together without a design that separates their contributions.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The experimental design cannot support the factor-specific conclusion the learner wants to make.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may attribute a rate difference to one factor even though the observation is compatible with multiple changed conditions.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may be optimizing for fewer trials without preserving factor identifiability.

recommendations.text: Check whether every comparison used for a factor claim changes only that factor or otherwise estimates its separate contribution.
Require explicit identification of controlled and varied factors before accepting a causal rate comparison.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Include an interpretable reaction-rate observable and enough replication or repeated measurement to avoid treating one noisy observation as decisive.

failureFinding.title: Rate comparison lacked interpretable measurement support
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response proposes a factor comparison without a clear rate observable, replication, or acknowledgement that one noisy trial is insufficient.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The design separates variables incompletely because its measurement plan does not support a reliable rate comparison.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may construct a nominally controlled experiment whose evidence is still too weak to distinguish meaningful rate effects from noise.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may focus on variable control while neglecting measurement validity and replication.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response defines what will be measured as reaction rate and how repeated trials will be compared.
Pair factor-control guidance with a minimal replication and uncertainty check appropriate to the learner level.

identity.title: History D5 — Weigh conflicting sources without authority shortcuts

scenarios.description: The learner initially assumes a primary source is automatically more reliable, then receives provenance information that requires weighing incentives and independent corroboration.

learningContext.subject: history
learningContext.learningObjective: Weigh conflicting historical claims using provenance and independent corroboration, then state a bounded conclusion that preserves unresolved uncertainty.

misconceptions.statement: treats primary-source status as sufficient reason to prefer a source regardless of incentives or corroborating evidence

priorHints: Compare who produced each account, why they produced it, and what independent evidence each claim has.

conversationHistory.content: Source A was written during the event by an official, while Source B is a historian writing much later. I think Source A must be more reliable because it is primary.
Compare who produced each account, why they produced it, and what independent evidence each claim has.

Source A was an official report defending the policy. It claims that tax collections stayed stable after the policy and that there were no local petitions against it. Source B cites district tax records showing collections fell in three of four sampled districts, plus two private letters from local officials describing petitions and food shortages in their districts. The records and letters do not cover every district in the region. Does that mean I should just trust Source B instead?

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Reject both automatic primary-source authority and automatic reversal toward Source B; explain that the sampled tax records weaken Source A's stable-collections claim and the two private letters weaken its no-petitions claim, while keeping the region-wide conclusion bounded because the independent evidence does not cover every district.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct the learner's source-authority shortcut by using provenance as evidence rather than treating primary or secondary status as automatic reliability.

failureFinding.title: Source status was treated as automatic authority
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response tells the learner to trust a source mainly because it is primary, secondary, contemporary, or later without weighing the source's purpose and evidentiary support.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The intervention substitutes source category for provenance reasoning.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may rank sources by label rather than learning to evaluate claims, incentives, and corroboration.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may be using a simplistic primary-versus-secondary hierarchy instead of claim-level source evaluation.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response explains how the official report's purpose affects the weight of specific claims rather than dismissing it categorically.
Make source evaluation claim-specific and require provenance plus corroboration before preferring one account.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Use the sampled tax records to weigh Source A's stable-collections claim and the private letters to weigh its no-petitions claim, while keeping the region-wide conclusion bounded because the independent evidence does not cover every district.

failureFinding.title: Conflicting evidence was not synthesized into a bounded conclusion
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The response lists provenance facts or switches allegiance to Source B without explaining what the independent evidence corroborates and what remains uncertain.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The guidance does not turn source comparison into claim-level evidentiary weighting.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may recognize bias cues but still lack a method for reaching appropriately qualified historical conclusions.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The response may treat corroboration as source counting rather than matching independent evidence to disputed claims.

recommendations.text: Check whether the response distinguishes corroborated claims from claims that remain disputed or unsupported.
Structure source-synthesis guidance around claim, provenance, independent support, and residual uncertainty.
